premise: You (second person) are a broke guy in a cheap rainy-city apartment who wins a $100 million lottery jackpot. Every part shows what really happens next and teaches one true money lesson through the story. Tone: tense, dry, a little funny, never preachy. The viewer decides the story at the end of each part by voting.
hero: You: about 30, works night shifts, rents a small apartment, close to your mom, never had money.

cast.mom: Your mom: warm, talks too much, lives in a small 1990s kitchen across town.
cast.cousin_mike: Cousin Mike: always has a business idea, texts too much.
cast.advisor: The man in the navy suit: a too-smooth financial salesman who showed up uninvited.

facts: Before claiming, big winners hire a team: a lawyer, a tax professional (CPA) and a fee-only fiduciary financial advisor.
A fiduciary adviser is legally required to act in your best interest; a salesman paid by commission is not.
Claim deadlines vary by state, commonly 180 days to a year, so there is time to prepare.
Advisors often charge around 1% of your money per year on smaller portfolios; on millions that is a lot, so ask how they are paid.
Only a handful of states let lottery winners stay anonymous by law.
Some states let a trust or company claim the prize, but in some of them the trustee's name is still published.
Lotteries use winners' names and photos in press releases; reporters and scammers read them.
In 2026 you can give up to $19,000 per person per year without filing a gift tax return.
Above $19,000 you file IRS Form 709, but you pay no gift tax until you pass the lifetime exemption of $15 million (2026).
A loan to family should be written down; an unwritten loan is usually a gift that never comes back.
State tax on lottery winnings depends on where you live.
Florida, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington and Wyoming do not tax lottery winnings; California does not tax its own state lottery prizes.
New York's top rate is 10.9%, and New York City adds up to 3.876% more.
Real prizes are free: anyone who asks you to pay a fee or 'taxes' up front to release a prize is a scammer (FTC).
Real taxes go to the IRS and the state, never to a 'prize agent' or a stranger on the phone.
Scammers watch lottery press releases and social media for new winners' names.
The famous claim that 70% of lottery winners go broke has no research behind it; NEFE, the group it is blamed on, says it cannot confirm it.
A real study (Hankins, Hoekstra and Skiba, 2011) of Florida winners of $50,000 to $150,000 found the win delayed bankruptcy but did not prevent it.
Money does not fix spending habits; a budget and a plan do.
The 4% rule (Bengen, 1994): withdrawing 4% in year one, adjusted for inflation, historically lasted at least 30 years.
4% of $38 million is $1.52 million a year.
At 3% inflation, prices double in about 24 years (rule of 72), so money left in cash slowly shrinks.
Umbrella liability insurance costs a few hundred dollars a year per million of coverage and protects rich people from lawsuits.
This is the series finale: the story ends, no vote, invite viewers to follow for the next series.
